title: Anna Karenina
synopsis: Imperial Russia. All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way. You're about to make a new way.

nodes.text: You come to Moscow to talk your brother's wife out of leaving him, which you will do successfully, and which will take four days. On the platform there is a crowd where a crowd should not be. A watchman has gone under the wheels in the yard. Someone says he was drunk. Someone says he had a family. You give money for the widow before you have your gloves off.

choices.consequence: You let yourself feel the cold of it standing there, and you will remember the exact sound the crowd made going quiet for the rest of your life.
You call it an accident, tip the porter, and walk out into the snow, and it is the last hour in which you are merely a woman visiting her brother.

nodes.text: He hands his mother down from the carriage, turns, and sees you, and for a moment neither of you does anything at all. It lasts less than a second and is entirely sufficient. Afterward you are extremely charming to the old countess and discuss the Petersburg weather at some length, and the whole time a part of you stands very still, waiting to be spoken to again.

choices.consequence: You cut it short, take your brother's arm, and walk faster than necessary, as proof of a discipline you will no longer possess by February. You withdraw. The decision moves you toward Karenin and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.
You stay in the noise of the platform three minutes past any reason for staying, and you know precisely what you are doing the entire time you do it.

nodes.text: Alexei Alexandrovich meets your train with his hat in his hand and asks whether the journey tired you. His ears stick out. You notice this now, which you did not notice for nine years. He tells you about a committee report at length, and he tells it kindly, meaning it as a gift: here is my day, I have carried it home to you. You cannot look at him.

choices.consequence: You give him the whole of Moscow, including the name, and he receives it as information and asks whether the samovar has been lit. You tell him plainly. The decision moves you toward Ball and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

You edit one man out of a four-day account. The lie is small and easy and takes no effort at all, and it is immediately permanent. You choose to withhold. It opens the route to Ball, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Kitty has been planning this evening since October. She wears white and pink and expects to be proposed to before supper. You wear black velvet because you had not intended to be looked at. Vronsky comes across the floor past her, past everybody, and asks you for the mazurka, and the room performs not noticing. Kitty stands with her dance card open in her hand, watching your face.

choices.consequence: You send for the carriage before supper and go, and it changes nothing whatever except that Kitty is ill for six weeks instead of two. You choose to leave early. It opens the route to St. Petersburg, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

You dance it, and let yourself be delighted, in a white dress with a girl of eighteen watching from against the wall. You choose to dance. It opens the route to St. Petersburg, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Seryozha is at the door in his sailor collar with his hair wet-combed by a nurse who wants credit for it. He is eight. He comes at your knees and puts his face into your skirts and asks what you brought him before he asks anything else at all. You brought him a wooden horse. Down the corridor your husband's study door is shut, and you are glad of it.

choices.consequence: You hold on to him until the nurse coughs, and it is standing in that hallway that you understand exactly what everything is going to cost. You commit to hold him long. By Races, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.
You set him on his feet, straighten the collar, and go up to change for dinner, and he stays in the hall a while longer looking at the door.

nodes.text: Seventeen officers, four miles, and the water jump at the far end where you cannot see clearly. Your husband sits beside you naming the families in the imperial box in order of precedence. The mare goes over badly and comes down on her back, and the sound reaches you half a second late, and you are on your feet with your hand at your mouth making a noise that everyone nearby hears.

choices.consequence: You sit, take up the glasses again, and remark on the weather in a level voice, and Karenin does not turn his head, which is considerably worse.
You do not arrange your face for anybody, and eight hundred people in the stands learn your private life in the time it takes a horse to fall.

nodes.text: In the carriage he says it without heat, as a man reads out a clause. The appearance of the thing is what concerns him. He will not divorce and he will not be humiliated. You may keep your position, your son, your house, and in exchange that man does not enter under his roof and you are not seen. Nothing else is required of you. Nothing at all is offered.

choices.consequence: You promise him everything he asks for and mean none of it, and he believes you, and it is the believing that you find you cannot forgive. You commit to lie. By Italy, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

You say it in six words in a moving carriage, and he goes on looking out of the window, and the horses do not change their pace. You tell the truth. The decision moves you toward Italy and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: A rented palazzo with cold floors and a landlord who overcharges you for firewood. Vronsky has taken up painting and is competent at it, which is the trouble; he can see exactly how far short of good he stands. You read in the afternoons. Nobody calls. Nobody cuts you, because nobody here knows what you are. For a month it is very nearly an ordinary life.

choices.consequence: You stretch the month into five, and by the last of them he rides out alone in the mornings and comes back with nothing at all to report. You stay months. The decision moves you toward Annie and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

You begin mentioning Petersburg in the evenings, and every single time you do it he agrees a shade too quickly. You choose to plan a return. It opens the route to Annie, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: The baby is dark and healthy and belongs more to a nursemaid than to you. You sit with her and do all the correct things and wait to feel what you felt in a hallway in Petersburg with a boy in a sailor collar, and it does not arrive. You love her the way you love a house taken for the season. You do not say this to a living person, ever.

choices.consequence: You take her mornings from the nurse and do it properly for weeks, and the feeling still does not come, and you stop holding it against her.

You leave her to the nursery and let the guilt settle somewhere behind your ribs, where by now it has a great deal of company. You don't try. The decision moves you toward Return to Russia and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: The verdict was passed while you were on the Adriatic. Invitations are not refused; they are simply not sent. Betsy comes once, stays twenty minutes, looks at the clock twice. Your name is now a thing said in a particular tone at tables you used to sit at. Vronsky's name is not. His club is precisely as pleased to see him as it was before, and he does not notice.

choices.consequence: You decide to go on the boy's birthday, before dawn, bribing a servant to open a house in which you know the number of stairs by heart. You visit Seryozha. The decision moves you toward Seryozha and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

You stay away for his sake and tell yourself so twice a day, and the argument gets weaker every single time you make it. You choose to avoid Seryozha. It opens the route to Seryozha, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: You get in at seven in the morning by the back stairs. He is half asleep and does not question your being there, and that is the unbearable part: he simply folds into you as though this happened every week. He tells you about a boy at his school. Then footsteps in the passage, and your husband's man in the doorway, embarrassed, waiting. Nine minutes altogether.

choices.consequence: You promise him you will come again, out loud, to his face, and it is the last outright lie you will ever tell a child. You vow to find a way. The decision moves you toward Salon and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

You put your forehead into his hair and ask for something without words, from a God you stopped consulting somewhere outside Florence. You pray. The decision moves you toward Salon and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You go to the opera in a low gown because staying home would be an admission, and Vronsky asks you not to, and you go. Madame Kartasova, in the next box, looks directly at you, says something to her husband, and leaves. The entire tier watches her leave. The soprano continues; she has been paid to. You sit through two more acts with your chin exactly level.

choices.consequence: You stay to the end and applaud in the correct places, and you go on paying for those two acts every night for the next six months. You commit to hold your shoulders. By Levin's Wedding, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

You go in the interval, and the carriage is silent all the way home, and in the hall he says one wrong sentence and the night comes apart. You choose to leave. It opens the route to Levin's Wedding, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: Somewhere in Moscow, in a church you will never enter, Kitty marries a landowner who nearly gave up farming out of despair. He is late; he cannot find a clean shirt. The whole business reaches you in a letter, as gossip, between two paragraphs about a hat. They are happy in a way that is neither interesting nor available to you, and they go on being happy for years at the edge of your life.

choices.consequence: You send silver, unsigned by Vronsky, and Kitty writes back three warm lines that you keep in a drawer and take out more often than you admit.

You send nothing, because any note would have to explain itself, and you have run entirely out of explanations. You commit to be still. By Jealousy, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: It begins as a habit of noticing which letters he opens with his back turned. Then it is the salver in the hall. Then the pockets of the coat his man has only just taken. There is never anything in them. This is not a relief; it means only that you have not found it yet. You begin asking him questions to which you already know the answers.

choices.consequence: You put the letter back unread and stand in the hall shaking, and you manage it for nine days, which is longer than you had any right to expect.

You read every line and find nothing, and the nothing convinces you of a carefulness that would have taken him months of practice. You commit to continue. By Morphine, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: The doctor gave it to you after Annie, for sleeplessness, in a small bottle with a printed label, entirely respectable. Now the evenings are unendurable without it and the mornings are worse. It does not make you happy. It puts the hours underwater and some distance off, where his voice cannot get all the way in. You have started measuring the dose in the dark without a light.

choices.consequence: You halve it for a week and sleep four hours a night and are unbearable to everyone in the house, and it is the last honest thing you attempt.

You take enough to blur the evening out entirely, and wake at four with your heart going, absolutely certain of things that are not true. You commit to take more. By Quarrel, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: It begins over whether you are going down to the country and ends somewhere else entirely, as everything now does. He puts on his coat and says he has business in Moscow with his mother, and it is the word mother that does it. He is gone by noon. His letter arrives Thursday: four lines, correct, affectionate in roughly the way a receipt is affectionate.

choices.consequence: You write something with a blade in the third sentence and send it before you can reconsider, and then spend the whole of the day at the window.

You write asking him to come back, plainly, with no pride left in it anywhere, and the plainness frightens you more than the anger did. You commit to send a soft one. By Train Station, Again, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

nodes.text: You have the carriage brought at five. Annushka asks whether you are ill and you say you are going out. The streets are full of ordinary people spending ordinary afternoons: a shop boy with a hoop, two women laughing at an upstairs window, a man carrying a mirror. Each of them looks to you like a person who has never once had to decide anything. You say: the station.

choices.text: Wait at the station for the next train
choices.consequence: You sit on a bench beneath the board with your ticket unbought, watching the hands move, doing absolutely nothing for forty minutes. You commit to wait at the station for the next train. By Platform, the choice has already shifted who trusts you and who begins to watch.

You send for a cab to take you out to him directly, and while you wait for it his telegram arrives, and it contains nothing you needed. You take a cab. The decision moves you toward Platform and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: The bell. Porters, a family arguing about a hatbox, a peasant in a filthy coat working at something down by the rails with an iron bar. The faces come apart into features and for a moment nothing means anything. Your shawl is heavy and your bag is heavy and your head has that underwater brightness. You take three steps toward the edge of the platform for no reason you could name.

choices.consequence: You take one step in the other direction, and the entire remainder of your life turns on a movement that nobody on the platform notices. You step back. The decision moves you toward Bookend and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

You move closer to the edge and the engine noise becomes very large, and everything else in the world becomes small and easily set down. You choose to step forward. It opens the route to Bookend, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.

nodes.text: There was a man under the wheels in this yard four years ago, on the day you came to save a marriage, and you paid for his widow before you had your gloves off. It has come round. Everything in your life has been a circle drawn slowly enough that you could not see the curve. Somewhere in all this noise a version of the next minute is still undecided.

choices.consequence: You reach for the other version with both hands and find it there, and it is not a rescue. It is only more time, which is not the same thing.

The world contracts to a candle and a page and the small sound of a book being closed. Nothing after this is yours to tell. You step. The decision moves you toward After and tells everyone present what you are willing to risk.

nodes.text: You are sitting on a bench with a porter asking twice whether you require assistance. Your hands will not be still and you put them under the shawl. You had believed the decision would arrive from outside you. It did not. Nobody was ever going to take the choice away and hold it for you. The train leaves. Another comes in twenty minutes, and you are still on the bench.

choices.consequence: You go back to the house you share with him and say nothing whatever about the afternoon, and you carry it privately for the next nine years.
You write him four sentences from the station hotel and take the southern train in the morning, frightened in a way that is entirely new and entirely your own.

nodes.text: Far off in a province you have never visited, Kitty's husband is mowing alongside his own peasants because he cannot think inside a house. The grass goes down in rows. He has been arguing with God since spring and losing, and this afternoon he stops minding that he is losing. He heard about you once at somebody's table. He thinks of you occasionally, without judgement, which is rarer than either.

choices.consequence: You write to a man you have never met about his wife's sister and the weather, and he keeps the letter, and you never learn that he kept it.

You leave the sheet blank, because there is nothing in you that can be said politely to a happy household. You choose to don't send. It opens the route to Step Back, giving up the protection of pretending you had not decided.
There has been a chapter running alongside yours the whole time, in hayfields and nurseries, and it does not require you in order to continue.

nodes.text: The book closes over you. There is a great deal of aftermath and none of it is yours. Vronsky, with his teeth ruined by pain and his mother saying unforgivable things in the next room, buys a company of volunteers and takes them into Serbia to be spent usefully. Karenin raises your son and your daughter under one roof, correctly, coldly, without a word of blame ever spoken aloud in the house. Seryozha grows up and does not discuss you. The trains keep running on that line, every hour, all winter.

You step back. It is not a redemption; it is a Tuesday. You take Annie and one maid to Italy and live in three rooms above a courtyard where a woman beats rugs at seven every morning. Society, having already finished with you, continues not to think of you. You read the newspapers four days late. In one, a small item: Count Vronsky has gone as a volunteer to Serbia. You set the paper down and go on with your morning. This is what surviving looks like from inside, and nobody writes it up.

Levin's chapter outlives yours. He gets his harvest in, and a son, and no answer whatever to the question. What he gets instead is the habit of getting up. He never resolves it. He is happy anyway, in the unspectacular manner that has never once made a plot. Once a year, out in the field when the light comes low and the mowing is going well, he thinks about the woman he met one evening in Moscow, understood entirely, and could not help. He never mentions it to Kitty.
